newsitem.title: JAPAN: Euro currency to challenge dollar supremacy-Chirac.
newsitem.headline: Euro currency to challenge dollar supremacy-Chirac.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, sticking to his theme that there is a new kid on the block to rival the United States in Asia, said on Tuesday the euro would one day challenge the dollar as the world's currency.

"I have to say, frankly, we have suffered from fluctuations of the dollar that do not always reflect economic reality and we need a currency (the euro) that is strong and powerful that would allow us to resist these aberrant fluctuations in the dollar," he told a group of business leaders.
Many in the English-language press, he said, were already more worried about what the single European currency would mean for the dollar than sceptical that the euro would happen.
A source close to the president earlier this week said many Japanese officials had told Chirac in private that a single European currency was needed to counterbalance the power of the dollar.

Though not specifically naming either the United States or Britain's Euro-sceptics in particular, Chirac said: "Europe will be tomorrow the economic power which is the most important in the world -- at least for sometime -- and of course that would worry certain (people) here and there."

He reassured his Japanese audience that France, Germany, Spain and Italy -- Britain was not named -- would make the Maastricht criteria for a single currency, one of part of which is to reduce budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"In two years, and despite difficult economic conditions, we have managed to reduce our public deficit from six percent to four percent of GDP and we will be at three percent next year," Chirac said.

"For too long in Europe, public deficits have discouraged initiative and pulled down the economy. It was time to break the vicious cycle," he said. "Yes, Germany, France, Italy and Spain will be there at the euro's rendezvous."
Since Chirac arrived in Japan on Sunday for a six-day visit, he has hammered home a message that it was time France and Europe seriously challenged U.S. business in Asia.
On Monday, Chirac signed an agreement entitled "20 Points For The Year 2000", designed to take Franco-Japanese relations to a higher plane.
It included agreements to hold annual summits, twice-yearly meetings of foreign ministers, and to increase cooperation in space research.
Also on Monday, he told students at Tokyo's Keio University that Japan had much to gain from close ties with Europe because the region was becoming an economic power reinforced by a single currency.
"That is why France is an essential partner for you," he said.
